name: HAL Dhruv Advanced Light Helicopter (ALH)

header.one_liner: India's indigenous twin-engine multirole helicopter; 300+ delivered across IAF, Indian Army, Indian Navy, Coast Guard; 34 on order end-FY26; Shakti engine from Safran (France) under licence.

what_it_is.prose: The HAL Dhruv Advanced Light Helicopter (ALH) is India's indigenous twin-engine multirole helicopter developed by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) with design support from Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm (MBB) of Germany in the 1980s-90s. The Dhruv entered service in 2002 and has been delivered to all three Indian armed services (IAF, Indian Army, Indian Navy) plus the Indian Coast Guard, with over 300 units delivered cumulatively. The helicopter is powered by two HAL/Safran (Turbomeca) Shakti turboshaft engines produced under licence by HAL with approximately 50% indigenous content. The Dhruv family comprises four main variants: Mk-I (basic transport), Mk-II, Mk-III (Maritime — for Indian Navy and Coast Guard with surface search radar, anti-ship missile capability, and emergency flotation), and Mk-IV WSI (Weapon System Integrated, designated Rudra — for the Indian Army with anti-tank guided missiles, rockets, and air-to-air missiles). The Dhruv has a Maximum Take-Off Weight of 5,500 kg, payload of 1,500 kg internal or 3,000 kg external, endurance of approximately 3.5 hours, and a service ceiling of 6,096 m (20,000 ft). HAL had 34 Dhruv ALH on order at the end of FY26 (part of the ₹2,54,538 crore order book). Export customers have included Mauritius, Nepal, and Ecuador (the latter experienced crashes that affected the export programme). The Dhruv has been deployed in combat roles including casualty evacuation, logistics supply, and Search and Rescue (SAR) — including during the 2015 Nepal earthquake relief and the 2020 Galwan Valley clash aftermath.

faq.question: What is the difference between Dhruv and Rudra?
faq.answer: Dhruv is the base Advanced Light Helicopter (ALH) platform. Rudra is the Dhruv Mk-IV WSI (Weapon System Integrated) variant for the Indian Army, equipped with anti-tank guided missiles, rockets, and air-to-air missiles. The Dhruv Mk-III Maritime variant is for the Indian Navy and Coast Guard, with surface search radar, anti-ship missile capability, and emergency flotation. All three share the same HAL airframe and Shakti engine.

faq.question: What engine powers the HAL Dhruv?
faq.answer: The HAL Dhruv is powered by two HAL/Safran (Turbomeca) Shaktu turboshaft engines produced under licence by HAL with approximately 50% indigenous content. The Shakti engine is the Indian designation for the Turbomeca TM333 2C2 (originally) and the Shakti (Ardiden 1H1) — the latter being the current production engine. The same Shakti engine also powers the Light Combat Helicopter (LCH) Prachand.

faq.question: Has the Dhruv been exported?
faq.answer: Yes. The Dhruv has been exported to Mauritius, Nepal, and Ecuador. The Ecuador programme was affected by multiple crashes, leading to operational concerns. HAL continues to market the Dhruv for export to friendly foreign countries, particularly in Southeast Asia, Africa, and Latin America. The Dhruv's combat-proven role in casualty evacuation (including during the 2015 Nepal earthquake relief) has been a key export selling point.
